Field Notes

South Asia is a region of extraordinary diversity, shaped by dramatic landscapes, ancient civilizations, powerful religions, and more than two billion people. The region includes India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, and the Maldives. From the towering Himalayas to fertile river valleys, crowded megacities, tropical islands, and rural farming villages, South Asia contains striking contrasts in both its physical and human geography. For thousands of years, trade, migration, conquest, and cultural exchange have connected the people of South Asia while creating distinct languages, religions, traditions, and identities. Understanding South Asia means recognizing both the diversity within the region and the geographic connections that unite it.

The Physical Landscape

South Asia is defined by dramatic physical contrasts. The Himalayas form a massive natural barrier along the region’s northern edge, while the fertile plains of the Indus, Ganges, and Brahmaputra river systems support some of the world’s largest concentrations of people. Farther south, the Deccan Plateau covers much of peninsular India, while Sri Lanka and the Maldives extend into the Indian Ocean. These rivers provide water for farming and daily life, and their fertile floodplains have supported large settlements for thousands of years. However, seasonal flooding can threaten communities, farmland, and infrastructure, particularly in low-lying areas such as Bangladesh.

The monsoon is one of the region’s most important physical processes. Seasonal winds bring rainfall that farmers depend on for crops and communities rely on for water, but unusually heavy or weak monsoons can contribute to floods, landslides, drought, and food shortages. Earthquakes in the Himalayan region, tropical cyclones along the coast, and rising sea levels also create significant challenges for communities across South Asia.

People and Population

South Asia is one of the most densely populated regions on Earth and is home to roughly one-fourth of the world’s population. However, people are not distributed evenly. Fertile river valleys and coastal plains contain extremely dense settlements, while the Himalayas, deserts, and other difficult environments have much smaller populations. India is the world’s most populous country, while countries such as Pakistan continue to have relatively youthful and growing populations. Differences in fertility rates, age structure, life expectancy, and migration mean that population challenges are not the same throughout the region.

Millions of people are also moving from rural communities into cities in search of education, employment, and economic opportunities, contributing to the rapid growth of cities such as Delhi, Mumbai, Dhaka, and Karachi. Rapid urbanization creates opportunities but can also place tremendous pressure on housing, transportation, sanitation, and water supplies. Migration also extends beyond the region: millions of South Asians live and work abroad, particularly in the Persian Gulf, Europe, and North America, and the money they send home, called remittances, is an important source of income for many families and national economies.

Political Aspects

India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and the Maldives are republics with elected governments, while Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy. The region’s modern political geography was heavily influenced by British colonial rule. When British rule ended in 1947, British India was divided primarily into India and Pakistan in an event known as Partition. Millions of Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs crossed the newly created borders, resulting in one of the largest migrations in human history. Bangladesh later became independent from Pakistan in 1971.

The effects of these changing borders are still visible today. Kashmir, a mountainous territory claimed by both India and Pakistan, has remained a source of tension between the two countries. Political relationships can also be influenced by borders, religion, ethnic identity, access to resources, and historical conflicts. Despite these challenges, countries throughout the region also cooperate through trade, diplomacy, transportation, and regional organizations.

Economic Aspects

South Asia contains some of the world’s fastest-growing economies, but levels of economic development vary greatly across and within countries. Agriculture remains an important source of employment, with farmers producing rice, wheat, tea, cotton, spices, sugarcane, and other crops. Manufacturing and services have expanded rapidly: India has become a global center for information technology, pharmaceuticals, business services, and software development, while Bangladesh is a major producer of clothing and textiles. Cottage industries also remain important in some communities, where families produce textiles, pottery, jewelry, and rugs in homes or small workshops. Tourism provides another source of income, with visitors traveling to Nepal for the Himalayas, Sri Lanka for its beaches and cultural sites, and the Maldives for its tropical islands.

Globalization has increasingly connected South Asia to the world economy through trade, foreign investment, outsourcing, tourism, and migration. Despite economic growth, poverty and inequality remain significant challenges, and access to education, healthcare, reliable electricity, clean water, and economic opportunities can differ considerably between urban and rural communities.

Social Aspects

South Asia is one of the most culturally diverse regions in the world, with hundreds of languages, religious traditions, and distinct cultural identities. Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, Punjabi, Tamil, Nepali, and Sinhala are among the major languages, while English is widely used in education, government, and business in several countries. The region is the birthplace of Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, and Jainism and is also home to one of the world’s largest Muslim populations. Religious beliefs influence architecture, festivals, food, clothing, family traditions, and daily routines, and celebrations such as Diwali, Eid, Vesak, and Holi illustrate the region’s religious and cultural diversity.

Family and community relationships remain important throughout much of South Asia, with extended families often maintaining close connections across generations. In India and Nepal, the historical caste system divided people into hereditary social groups that influenced occupations, marriage, and social relationships. India officially prohibits caste-based discrimination, although caste identity can still influence social experiences and opportunities in some communities today. Education is highly valued, although access varies considerably between countries and between urban and rural communities, and healthcare varies as well.

Food provides another window into the region’s diversity. Rice, wheat, lentils, vegetables, seafood, and spices form the foundation of many meals, but ingredients and traditions vary widely according to location, climate, religion, and local culture. South Asia also has rich traditions in music, dance, literature, textiles, architecture, and visual arts, alongside a thriving modern popular culture: India’s film industry, including Bollywood and numerous regional film industries, reaches audiences around the world. Cricket is especially popular and often serves as a shared cultural connection across national borders, even between countries that may otherwise experience political rivalry.

Region Activity

This region’s activity is completed as an assignment in Canvas. Read the overview below, then head to your Canvas assignment to begin.
Celebrations Across South Asia

Throughout South Asia, celebrations reflect the religious beliefs, traditions, and cultural identities of the people who live there. From Hindu weddings and Diwali celebrations in India, to Islamic traditions surrounding Eid al-Fitr in Pakistan, and Buddhist celebrations in Sri Lanka, these customs help us better understand the cultural diversity of this region.

For this activity, you will be randomly assigned one of four cultural celebrations to explore through an interactive field experience.
